title: "The Valet" ("La Doublure")
full_review:
"The Valet" ("La Doublure") (Sony Classics) is the latest French farce from writer-director Francis Veber who has previously given us such lightweight but amusing gems as "The Dinner Game," "The Toy" and "The Closet."

His latest farce -- thin but (some language flags aside) delightful as the others -- concerns nerdy restaurant parking valet Francois Pignon (Gad Elmaleh), who is paid to pretend he's having an affair with glamorous supermodel Elena (Alice Taglioni) after his image is accidentally captured behind her in a tabloid photograph showing the model with wealthy industrialist Pierre Levasseur (Daniel Auteuil), with whom she's romantically involved.

Pierre's crafty lawyer, Foix (Richard Berry), concocts the scheme after Pierre's wife, Christine (Kristin Scott Thomas), sees the photo and suspects the worst, knowing her errant husband all too well. (As Christine owns the lion's share of her husband's business, it's imperative to defuse her suspicions.)

Elena reluctantly agrees to the scheme with various provisions and, far from being a calculating vixen, actually helps Pignon woo childhood sweetheart Emilie (Virginie Ladoyen), a bookstore owner, whom he truly loves. And as time goes by, Pignon helps Elena see the wrongness of her affair with Levasseur.

Veber is a master at this sort of concoction, and like most classic farces, though it seems to be about amorous matters, nothing actually happens at all, and everything is resolved morally by the final fade-out.

The cast is fine. Interestingly, Auteuil played Pignon (Veber's Everyman character) in "The Closet." Talented young actor Dany Boon plays Pignon's sad-sack former roommate (and fellow valet) who imagines his buddy has become quite the ladies' man.

A brightly colored Paris and a cheerful background score add to the fun.

Like other Veber films, Hollywood has shown an interest in this one, with Variety reporting that DreamWorks has secured the rights as a Farrelly brothers' project. Given Tinseltown's track record with other Veber properties, the original is unlikely to be bettered.

Subtitles.

The film contains an instance of the f-word and some other crude language, innuendo, a prior adulterous affair and a chaste bedroom scene with an accidental groping. The USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG-13 -- parents strongly cautioned. Some material may be inappropriate for children under 13.
